items.rationale: A fully baked cake's toothpick carries a few moist crumbs but no wet batter; a completely dry, crumb-free toothpick usually means the cake has already overbaked past the point of doneness.

items.answer: It springs back when you press the center lightly.
accepted: The center springs back when touched instead of leaving a dent
It feels firm and springy in the middle, not wet or jiggly
The edges have started pulling away from the sides of the pan
items.rationale: A done cake's crumb has set enough to spring back under light pressure, and the edges begin to loosen from the pan; an underdone center leaves a dent that does not bounce back.

Opening the door drops the oven's heat right when the center is still rising and has not set; the structure loses the heat it needs to finish and collapses as it cools. Sinking is a sign of an interrupted or underbaked center, not something that happens on its own to a finished cake.

Once the toothpick shows moist crumbs, the cake is done; ten more minutes bakes off the moisture the crumb needs to stay tender. Overbaking, not a measuring slip or a cool oven, is the usual cause of a dry cake.

The batter touching the hot pan at the edges sets and stops rising first, while the insulated center is still expanding; with nowhere else to go, it pushes straight up into a dome. A dome by itself does not mean the center is raw -- check it with a toothpick the same way as the rest of the cake.

Classic butter, vanilla and chocolate layer cakes are fully baked around 205-210°F at the center. That is well below the oven's 350°F air temperature -- the oven setting and the cake's own doneness temperature are not the same number.
